newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, U.S. discuss diverting U.S. aid to Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Israel, U.S. discuss diverting U.S. aid to Jordan.

text.p: Finance Minister Dan Meridor discussed Israel's involvement in an aid programme for Jordan with U.S. Ambassador Martin Indyk on Tuesday, his office said.

"The meeting was initiated by the American ambassador and a number of issues were discussed, mainly the aid programme to Jordan and the question of Israel's participation in it," the Finance Ministry said in statement.

The meeting came as Israeli Deputy Finance Minister David Magen resigned, citing among other things what he said was Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's willingness to give up a portion of its U.S. aid in order that it go to Jordan.

Meridor has hinted at reservations over the plan, saying Israel's annual U.S. aid allocation of $3 billion in military and civilian aid is crucial when Israel is taking risks for peace with the Arab world.

Magen said in his first radio interview after resigning over what he called Netanyahu's "major screw-ups and mistakes" that the prime minister had agreed in secret talks with King Hussein on May 8 to give up $50 million in U.S. civilian aid in order that it go to Jordan.
On Friday, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright neither confirmed nor denied reports of a plan to increase U.S. aid to Jordan by diverting funds from the annual allocation to Israel.
Albright said President Bill Clinton discussed increasing aid to Jordan with Netanyahu, who was interested in what she called "a fund for Middle East peace and security".
Jordan received $47 million in economic and military aid in 1997. President Bill Clinton asked for $75.6 million in his 1998 budget request.
